title: J.S. Mill

cards.b:
John Stuart Mill (1806–1873) was educated by his father James Mill, a close ally of Jeremy Bentham, to be the next leader of utilitarianism. He learned Greek at three.

At twenty he had a breakdown and came to feel that pure calculation left out feeling and character. He then reshaped the utilitarian tradition.

His key works are On Liberty (1859), Considerations on Representative Government (1861), Utilitarianism (1861/1863) and The Subjection of Women (1869). UPSC asks most about liberty and representation.

Bentham said the right action brings the greatest happiness of the greatest number. All pleasures are equal in kind; only quantity matters.

Mill added quality. Higher pleasures of the mind are better than lower pleasures of the body.

"It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied."
J.S. Mill, Utilitarianism, ch. 2

This made his utilitarianism about developing human beings, not just counting pleasures.

The heart of On Liberty is one simple principle. The only purpose for which power can rightly be used over anyone against their will is to prevent harm to others.

A person's own good, physical or moral, is not enough reason. Over himself, over his own body and mind, "the individual is sovereign".

Mill divides actions into self-regarding (affecting mainly oneself) and other-regarding (affecting others). Only the second may be controlled.

Mill gives strong reasons why no opinion should be silenced:

  • The silenced opinion may be true. To silence it assumes we cannot be wrong.
  • Even if false, it may hold part of the truth.
  • Even a wholly true belief, if never challenged, becomes a dead dogma, held without understanding.

But speech that is a direct incitement can be stopped. His example: saying corn dealers starve the poor is allowed in print, but not when shouted to an angry mob outside a corn dealer's house.

Mill, influenced by Alexis de Tocqueville, feared a new danger in democracy. Not just the government, but society itself, could crush individuals through public opinion and custom.

He valued individuality and "experiments of living". Progress comes from people who think differently. Conformity makes society stagnate, as he believed had happened in China.

So liberty is not only about protecting rights. It is about letting human beings grow.

• The ideally best form of government is representative democracy. It protects people's interests and also educates and improves them.
  • He backed Thomas Hare's system of proportional representation, so that minorities are heard.
  • He proposed plural voting: more votes for the educated, to balance the uneducated majority.
  • Voters should be literate and pay tax. He opposed the secret ballot, saying voting is a public duty.
  • Parliament should debate and check; laws should be drafted by an expert commission.

Mill wrote this book in 1869, drawing on his partnership with Harriet Taylor Mill. He argued that the legal subordination of women was wrong in itself and a major barrier to human progress.

He said we cannot know women's "nature" while they are kept in subjection.

As an MP in 1867, he proposed an amendment to give women the vote, replacing "man" with "person" in the Reform Bill. It failed, but it was the first such motion in Parliament.

• The line between self- and other-regarding actions is blurry. Almost every act affects someone.
  • Plural voting and the call for education tests are elitist.
  • He said liberty applies only to people in the "maturity of their faculties". Despotism is fine for "barbarians", he said, if it improves them. He worked for the East India Company for 35 years and defended its rule over India.
  • Yet he moved toward a qualified socialism in later life, so many see him as a bridge from classical to welfare liberalism. Ernest Barker was harsher: he called Mill the prophet of an empty liberty and an abstract individual.

cards.h: Positive views of liberty in Mill
cards.b:
Mill is often called the great defender of negative liberty: freedom from interference. But he goes further.

Chapter 3 of On Liberty is about individuality as part of well-being. Human nature, he says, is not a machine built to a model. It is a tree that needs to grow on all sides.

He quotes the German thinker Wilhelm von Humboldt, who said the end of man is the fullest and most harmonious development of his powers.

So Mill's liberty is not just about being left alone. It is about self-development. This is why he is seen as a bridge to T.H. Green and positive liberty.

He also allowed state action where it helps people develop, such as compulsory education. The state can require children to be educated, though it need not run all the schools.

Article 19(1)(a) protects free speech, but Article 19(2) lists reasonable restrictions such as public order and decency. This is close to Mill's harm-based approach.

In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act. It separated discussion and advocacy, which are protected, from incitement, which can be restricted. This echoes Mill's corn-dealer example.

In Navtej Johar (2018), decriminalising consensual same-sex relations reflected the idea that private self-regarding conduct is not the state's business.

"Mill was a reluctant democrat." Comment.
"Explain Mill's harm principle and its relevance today."
"Mill's liberalism is a bridge between classical and welfare liberalism." Discuss.

Structure: revised utilitarianism, the harm principle, three arguments for free speech, tyranny of the majority, representative government. Then critique (elitism, colonial blind spot) and Indian cases.

quiz.q: Mill's harm principle says power over an individual is justified only to…
quiz.w: The only purpose is to prevent harm to others.

quiz.q: Mill's change to Bentham's utilitarianism was to add…
quiz.w: Higher pleasures are better than lower ones, not just more pleasure.

quiz.q: Whose system of proportional representation did Mill support?
quiz.w: Mill backed Thomas Hare's single transferable vote system.

quiz.q: Mill's corn dealer example shows the line between…
quiz.w: The same words are allowed in print but not as incitement to an angry mob.

quiz.q: Which Indian case echoes Mill's line between advocacy and incitement?
quiz.w: Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down Section 66A using this distinction.
A tree that must grow and develop on all sides.

quiz.q: Mill's idea of individuality was influenced by…
quiz.w: He quotes Humboldt on the harmonious development of human powers.
Plural voting, and he opposed the secret ballot.

quiz.q: The Subjection of Women was published in…

quiz.w: Following Tocqueville, he feared majority opinion would crush individuality.
